newsitem.title: CONGO: Shooting erupts around Brazzaville airport.
newsitem.headline: Shooting erupts around Brazzaville airport.

text.p: Shooting erupted around Brazzaville international airport early on Sunday, ending two days of calm in the fighting between supporters of the Congo Republic's president and its former Marxist military leader.

Mortar fire began at around 2 a.m. near the airport and the aviation club where French troops are based in what a Western military source said was an assault by Denis Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia to take the airport from President Pascal Lissouba's forces.
By 7 a.m. the shooting had intensified with small arms and machinegun fire and black smoke rose from the airbase next to the airpot where Lissouba loyalist troops are based.
"It appears pretty evident that this is an attempt by Sassou Nguesso to take the airport," the Western military source said.
He said the militiamen were also using a tank in their assault.
French army spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said the militia forces were about 500 metres (yards) from the French base, but there was no need for the French to open fire to push them back.
"The (militia) are using 100mm mortar and firing at the army positions at the airbase at the far side of the airport," Pelissier said.

The area around the airport and the battered capital had been relatively calm in the past two days as mediators focused on ways of halting political and ethnic bloodshed and organising promised presidential elections.

The conflict started on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election. Lissouba's mandate ends of August 31.

Envoys representing Lissouba and his predecessor and arch rival Sassou Nguesso agreed on Saturday to meet in Gabon to for talks on implementing a peace deal -- with deployment of an African force being touted as one solution.

Confusion surrounded the timing of the talks. Brazzaville mayor and mediator Bernard Kolelas said the envoys would meet on Sunday. Others mediators and sources in Gabon's capital Libreville said the talks would most likely be on Monday.

"We must do everything to ensure that the elections are held within the delays foreseen in the constitution," U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said after talks with all sides. "Democracy must definitely be put back on track," he said.

The two sides declared a truce on Wednesday and only occasional explosions and shooting was heard in the centre of the oil-producing former French colony's capital on Saturday. Friday too was comparatively quiet.

Bodies litter Brazzaville's streets and the smell of rotting corpses permeates parts of the city. Some sources say the death toll could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand but many of the dead lay uncollected where they fell.
Soldiers supporting Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso's militiamen spent much of Saturday drinking beer or casually looting.
At Sassou Nguesso's heavily fortified home, one stop on Sahnoun's shuttle around town, a young militiaman held an AK-47 in one hand and a selection of children's toys in the other.

Sahnoun, travelling in an armoured car and protected by French special forces commandos, crossed battle lines in the city, passing buildings smashed by rockets and looters. Fires smouldered in some as dusk closed in.
France, which has evacuated almost 5,000 foreign nationals, about a third of them French, says that it will wind up its rescue mission on Sunday and start pulling out.
Sahnoun said that one idea on the table was for an African peace force. "We are going to discuss this issue," he said. "We don't rule out an African presence."
Lissouba told Gabon-based Africa Number One radio he favoured deployment of an African force, "possibly led by France with whom we are used to working, to guarantee the elections".
Sassou Nguesso, whose Cobra militia made some gains during last week's fighting, said he was not opposed the idea -- "on condition that it (the force) does not become permanent."
He too has called for elections to go ahead. "On the eve of the polling, passions must be cooled and conditions created for fair and transparent elections," he said.
